terms.gloss: stand on one’s hands: do a handstand
terms.grammar: stō, stāre, stetī, statum, with the ablative manibus
terms.comment: A description of ours: we have found no word for a handstand in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini. It is built like dextrō pede stāre, stand on one’s right foot (Traupman 57), and like Cicero’s manibus ingredī, walk on one’s hands.

terms.grammar: ingredior, ingredī, ingressus sum, with the ablative manibus
evidence: Cic. Fin. 5.35: ut sī aut manibus ingrediātur quis aut nōn ante, sed retrō
terms.comment: Cicero’s example of a movement against nature, beside walking backwards: the classical phrase for walking on one’s hands.

phrases.latin: Potesne manibus stāre? Pedēs tuōs teneō.
phrases.english: Can you do a handstand? I’ve got your feet.
Walk on your hands, if you can!

phrases.latin: ut sī aut manibus ingrediātur quis aut nōn ante, sed retrō
phrases.english: as if someone were to walk on his hands, or not forwards but backwards

sources: Lewis & Short: sto · Lewis & Short: ingredior · Lewis & Short: manus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 57.
